newsitem.title: CHINA: Red-chip fever no cure-all for China state firms.
newsitem.headline: Red-chip fever no cure-all for China state firms.

text.p: China's ailing state firms may not find public stock sales to be the answer to their financial woes, despite the huge success of the offer by Beijing Enterprises, a senior economic analyst said on Friday.
"Not that many companies will be able to do this," said Li Qiming, senior statistician of the State Statistical Bureau. "We should remain calm about this," he told reporters.
Beijing Enterprises Holdings' shares surged to HK$40.20 ($5.20) at the close on its trading debut on the Hong Kong stock exchange on Thursday from their offer price of HK$12.48.
The offer was more than 1,000 times oversubscribed and hundreds of thousands of application forms for the offer were quickly snatched up by eager investors.
Beijing Enterprises, a Hong Kong company controlled by the Beijing municipal government, has profitable operations, something many of China's state companies lack.
It has interests in toll roads, a highly successful brewery and the McDonald's outlets in the nation's capital.
Other red chips, or companies based in Hong Kong but mainly representing assets in China, have also been much sought after by Hong Kong's investing public.
But for most state-run Chinese enterprises, the story is much different.
China's state-run companies have struggled to compete in the sink-or-swim marketplace that emerged under ambitious economic reforms begun in 1979.

The state has been forced to subsidise these debt-saddled firms, but it wants to reduce its financial burden and modernise these companies to give them the means to compete with more nimble private sector rivals.
That would mean either layoffs of bloated state payrolls or bankruptcies, but Communist Party leaders are fearful this could create social instability.
Li said he believed that at least 15 percent of the nation's 88,000 state-run companies, many of which have been unable to reverse persistent losses, should eventually be allowed to go bankrupt.

"In my personal view, this could take five years," he said, adding that the pace of bankruptcies would be linked to the speed in which a national social security and unemployment insurance system was put in place.
China has no national system to provide for displaced or retired workers. That responsibility largely falls to the employer, and bankruptcies could cut off benefits to millions of workers.
At the end of the first quarter of this year, about 46 percent of the nation's state-run enterprises were losing money.
Li did not give a figure for the number of workers who would be thrown out of their jobs if these struggling state firms were allowed to go out of business.

But he said most of these were smaller companies and the total of displaced workers would be less than 15 percent of the workforce of state firms, which he estimated at a total of 46.5 million people.
Some 19 million of those workers already were on reduced salaries because of economic difficulties, he said. ($1 = HK$7.73
